title: Jay Worthy & George Clinton Are Bringing Funk Back to Rap: ‘It’s Getting Ready to Get Deep Around Here’
summary: The West Coast MC linked up with the funk pioneer to try and rectify G-Funk with their collab album Generation P.
contentText:
Jay Worthy wants to bring the funk back to rap.

So naturally, the Compton MC (by way of Vancouver) took advantage of a chance DM from George Clinton ‘s grandson, Zavier Croft. What resulted from the exchange is a 12-song collab album between LNDN DRGS and Clinton that features P Worthy rapping over some of Parliament-Funkadelic ‘s greatest hits, like “(Not Just) Knee Deep” and “Atomic Dog” with the help of producer Sean House as the funk legend himself provides some much needed narration.

This all got put in motion because Croft was playing a Jay Worthy & Larry June project while on the road with his grandfather. “We were on tour a couple years ago, and I was playing 2 P’z in the Pod , and I believe I was playing ‘Maybe the Next Time,'” Zavier says over Zoom. “And George was like, ‘Yo, yo, who is that? Let’s see what they’re up to.’ So then I reached out to Jay Worthy, and as soon as I DM’d him and told him who I was, he asked for my phone number and FaceTimed me. After that it was just a snowball effect of working together and building this.”

Worthy and House were then presented with a batch of songs that were cleared for use and started crafting what would become Generation P. Once they had something to present, LNDN DRGS headed out to play what he had for George out in Tallahassee, Florida. “I hit up management for songs that George and Parliament own so we can sample them without legal issues or getting in trouble, so that George and the band can benefit from,” Croft tells me. “There were a couple of albums I already knew that we could use, like Uncle Jam Wants You and One Nation Under a Groove . I sent it to Jay and we talked through it. That’s how it all worked out.”

“I linked up with Sean, and then we made that trip down to Tallahassee, and G was f—king with it,” Worthy adds. “He P’d on it and I P’d on it, and then we took it back to L.A. and I started getting them features on it, and then I went back to Tallahassee and played it for them after it was all done. It’s been about like three years, man. For real.” Once they were ready to go, they leaned into the nostalgia and released a 16-bit video game entitled P of the Week — a mix of Super Mario Bros. and Streets of Rage — during the rollout.

Like Worthy’s Once Upon A Time double disc from last year, Generation P bridges the gap of California’s deep rap lineage with features from Snoop Dogg , Larry June , 03 Greedo , Kokane, Ty Dolla $ign , Channel Tres , Terrace Martin , YG, The Game , Ab-Soul , Aceyalone and Del the Funky Homosapien. During our talk, George raved about Jay’s work ethic, because it reminded him of himself. “Y’all remind me of remind me of those old-school days of hustlin’,” he said on several occasions with a big smile on his face and a blunt in his hand. The 85-year-old legend is still clearly having fun making music.

Check out Billboard ‘s conversation with the newfound collaborators below.

This is a a random question, but do you rep Jersey or do you rep Cali? Because I’m from Jersey too, and was always curious. I grew up in Paterson.

George Clinton: Yeah, I rep the planet, man. But I used to hang around for Passaic and Englewood and Hackensack, you know? I grew up in Newark, and worked in Plainfield most of my life. But musically, the the tracks of the funk leads you to L.A. and Detroit.

Your sound is so synonymous with L.A., thanks to guys like DJ Quik and Warren G and Dr. Dre and them.

G.C.: You know, the high-frequency synthesizer sound of P-Funk in the records we made was big in L.A. The Funkadelic stuff was really big in New York City — Bronx, Brooklyn — all of that. So, you got the different styles of P-Funk in different places, and those two were the main ones.

When it comes to clearing samples for rappers, you have a reputation for being easy to work with compared to other older acts of your stature. Sometimes, they give rappers a hard time when they want to sample stuff. What is it about hip-hop that you love so much?

G.C.: The way I look at it is, if it’s gonna be, it’s gonna be. That was the next era that was gonna be. That was the reality of it, so I wasn’t gonna fight against what was gonna be the reality of the next set of music that was coming along. I always try to go with the flow — but there’s something to not letting it, because it’s hard to get paid for doing it. A lot of people are afraid of not getting paid, or didn’t know how they was going to get paid. I’d rather take the chance, and go on the side of this new thing, and we’ll figure that out later.

The record business has always been a hustle right from the beginning, that’s just now trying to clean itself up and get legal and all that. I’m glad I’m still around, because I still got a chance to get paid.

So, Jay, how did you feel about getting that DM and how did you guys end up doing an entire project together?

Jay Worthy: I was shocked, you know what I’m saying? Because George is one of my biggest influences. So, once I tapped in and it was real, we all got on the line. And actually, Zavier invited me out to the Spinning Gold movie premiere.

Zavier Croft: It was crazy, because we ended up being in a room — and it was me, Jay, Wiz, and Bishop Don Juan. We have so many stories but that was the first time being together.

J.W.: Then we went to George’s show, and Quik was there, which led to me working with Quik and executive producing his album — because he’s like, “S—t, if George is f—kin’ with you, I’m I’m not stopping the floodgates.” So, I’m very thankful for George trusting me and Sean with the sound and with his catalog and letting us do what we do. We went to work right away.

So, Jay, once you had songs to choose from, how did you and Sean approach making them? Were there any live instruments involved, or did you guys go for straight loops?

J.W.: Me and Sean like keeping the s—t pure, you know what I’m saying? That’s always been our sound. You know the motto: Don’t fix it if it ain’t broken. Them s—ts was already hits, and already slapping. We kept it raw. We didn’t add anything to any of those records.

G.C.: And they didn’t really have to sample, because we had access to the whole 24-track, so we could use any part of the whole thing. These were tracks from the original sessions, you didn’t have to loop anything — because half of the stuff was looped already. “Knee Deep” is 20 minutes long. We looped it ourselves when we did it.

So, you rap over certain parts of the songs.

J.W.: Exactly.

G.C.: Right. They came in on sections of the songs, but the songs are actually as they originally sound.

Yeah, they sound that. It reminded me of when Ghostface raps over an R&B track with the vocals and all that.

G.C.: That’s how Dre did it on The Chronic .

But then you also got Terrace Martin on there. Talk about adding someone like him to the mix — someone who plays live instruments.

J.W.: That’s my boy — but also I just feel like Terrace is the face of jazz when it comes down to the youth right now. Also [with] the works he’s done with Kendrick, SZA and TDE. I was able to play this record to Kendrick before it came out, and I was able to get Terrace’s ear on this, and he loved it and wanted to be a part of it. And I was honored to have Terrace a part of it. I think he added something great to it. He put that jazz on it, and that’s what was cool to me.

So actually, when you asked, did we add any instruments to the album? We did with Terrace on the saxophone… and then Channel Tres played a little bit of keys on the intro to “Oh I.”

Yo…
